179:   are not a final result.
180: - The independent pre-freeze review checks every E and complete P, including
181:   hypotheses, quantifiers and relevant definitions. Final machine Audit B checks
182:   actual exported full types and complete closure against that frozen authority.
183:   Supply short direct/equivalent correspondence explanations. Check actual Lean
184:   closure and trust, without a Mathlib-to-NL0 use ledger.
185:   Neither author notes nor a compiler pass are semantic approval.
186: - Stop on a judged substantive mathematical gap. Ordinary expansion and local
187:   verifiable corrections remain allowed. Difficulty or elapsed time does not
188:   establish that a mathematical claim is false.

1: # Irreducibility after reduction of an admissible sl2 lattice
2: 
3: ## Original exercise
4: 
5: James E. Humphreys, *Introduction to Lie Algebras and Representation Theory*,
6: Graduate Texts in Mathematics 9, Springer, section 27, exercise 7,
7: printed page 164. The exercise-list convention on page 163 sets
8: \(L=\mathfrak{sl}_2\) and identifies weights with integers.
9: Book DOI: [10.1007/978-1-4612-6398-2](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4612-6398-2).
10: 
11: > 7. If \(0\leq\lambda<\operatorname{char}K\), \(V=V(\lambda)\),
12: > prove that \(V(K)\) is irreducible as \(L(K)\)-module.
13: 
14: ## Definitions and complete target
15: 
16: Let \(p\) be any prime, \(K\) any field of characteristic \(p\), and
17: \(\lambda\) an integer with \(0\leq\lambda<p\).
18: Let \(V(\lambda)\) be the complex irreducible highest-weight
19: \(\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)\)-module of highest weight \(\lambda\),
20: of dimension \(\lambda+1\). Its Chevalley generators satisfy
21: 
22: \[
23: [h,x]=2x,\qquad[h,y]=-2y,\qquad[x,y]=h.
24: \]
25: 
26: Choose a nonzero highest-weight vector \(v\) with \(xv=0\) and
27: \(hv=\lambda v\). Let \(U_{\mathbb Z}\) be the integer subalgebra of
28: the universal enveloping algebra generated by all divided powers
29: \(X_r=x^r/r!\), \(Y_r=y^r/r!\), for integers \(r\geq0\).
30: An **admissible lattice** \(M\subset V(\lambda)\) is a free abelian
31: subgroup with an integer basis that is also a complex basis, stable under
32: \(U_{\mathbb Z}\). It is arbitrary, not necessarily the minimal lattice.
33: 
34: Put \(V(K)=M\otimes_{\mathbb Z}K\). The Lie algebra
35: \(L(K)=(\mathbb Zx+\mathbb Zy+\mathbb Zh)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}K\)
36: acts by the induced lattice operators. This is the Chevalley
37: \(\mathfrak{sl}_2\) construction also in characteristic 2.
38: Prove that \(V(K)\) is nonzero and every \(K\)-linear subspace
39: invariant under \(x,y,h\) is zero or all of \(V(K)\).
40: Both \(\lambda=0\) and \(p=2\) are included; \(K\) need not be
41: algebraically closed.
42: 
43: ## Fixed natural-language proof
44: 
45: ### 1. Divided-power coordinates in characteristic zero
46: 
47: Put \(n=\lambda+1\) and \(e_i=y^iv/i!\) for \(0\leq i\leq\lambda\).
48: The commutator identities give, by induction,
49: 
50: \[
51: hy^iv=(\lambda-2i)y^iv,\qquad
52: xy^iv=i(\lambda-i+1)y^{i-1}v\quad(i\geq1).
53: \]
54: 
55: For \(i\leq\lambda\), applying \(x^i\) to \(y^iv\) gives
56: \(i!\lambda(\lambda-1)\cdots(\lambda-i+1)v\ne0\) over \(\mathbb C\).
57: At \(i=0\) the empty product is one. Thus every \(e_i\ne0\).
58: Their \(h\)-eigenvalues \(\lambda-2i\) are distinct over \(\mathbb C\),
59: so they are linearly independent: applying
60: \(\prod_{k\ne j}(h-(\lambda-2k)\mathrm{Id})\) to a relation isolates
61: its \(j\)-th coefficient with a nonzero multiplier.
62: There are \(n\) vectors, the dimension of \(V(\lambda)\), hence they
63: form a basis. Also \(y^{\lambda+1}v=0\), since otherwise it would be
64: an eigenvector of eigenvalue \(-\lambda-2\), absent from this basis.
65: All higher lowering powers vanish as well.
66: 
67: The operator matrices are therefore
68: 
69: \[
70: xe_0=0,\quad xe_i=(\lambda-i+1)e_{i-1}\ (i\geq1),\qquad
71: ye_i=(i+1)e_{i+1}\ (i<\lambda),\quad ye_\lambda=0,
72: \quad he_i=(\lambda-2i)e_i.
73: \]
74: 
75: Iteration gives the integral divided-power matrices
76: 
77: \[
78: X_re_i=\binom{\lambda-i+r}{r}e_{i-r}\quad(0\leq r\leq i),
79: \qquad
80: Y_re_i=\binom{i+r}{r}e_{i+r}\quad(i+r\leq\lambda).       \tag{1}
81: \]
82: 
83: The respective expressions are zero when \(r>i\) or
84: \(i+r>\lambda\), by termination of the strings just proved.
85: 
86: ### 2. Matrix units preserve the localized arbitrary lattice
87: 
88: Let \(R=\mathbb Z_{(p)}=\{a/b\in\mathbb Q:p\nmid b\}\), and regard
89: \(M_R=R\otimes_{\mathbb Z}M\) as a submodule of \(V(\lambda)\).
90: The embedding is injective because an integer basis of \(M\) is
91: complex-linearly independent. The module \(M_R\) is free of rank \(n\)
92: over \(R\) and is preserved by all \(X_r,Y_r\), by admissibility.
93: 
94: Define \(E_{ij}\) to send \(e_j\) to \(e_i\) and all other basis
95: vectors to zero. Formula (1) gives
96: 
97: \[
98: P:=Y_\lambda X_\lambda=E_{\lambda\lambda},\qquad
99: X_{\lambda-i}P=E_{i\lambda},\qquad
100: P Y_{\lambda-j}=\binom\lambda j E_{\lambda j}.
101: \]
102: 
103: For the last identity, an input index below \(j\) is sent below
104: \(e_\lambda\) and killed by \(P\); an index above \(j\) is sent past
105: the end of the lowering string. On \(e_j\) the coefficient is precisely
106: \(\binom\lambda j\). Since \(\lambda<p\), none of
107: \(\lambda!\), \(j!\), \((\lambda-j)!\) is divisible by \(p\), so
108: \(\binom\lambda j\) is a unit in \(R\). Consequently
109: 
110: \[
111: E_{ij}=\left(\binom\lambda j\right)^{-1}
112:        X_{\lambda-i}P Y_{\lambda-j}.                 \tag{2}
113: \]
114: 
115: Every matrix unit preserves \(M_R\). No assertion about distinct
116: weights modulo \(p\) has been used.
117: 
118: ### 3. Recover a standard basis for the arbitrary lattice
119: 
120: Define \(J_i=\{c\in\mathbb C:c e_i\in M_R\}\).
121: The coordinate projection \(E_{ii}\) maps \(M_R\) onto \(J_i e_i\).
122: Applying \(E_{ij}\) to \(c e_j\) shows \(J_j\subseteq J_i\);
123: reversing the indices gives equality. Let \(J\) be their common module.
124: It is finitely generated, being a projection of a finite free module,
125: and nonzero because \(M_R\) spans \(V(\lambda)\) over \(\mathbb C\).
126: The coordinate projections and independence of the \(e_i\) give
127: 
128: \[
129: M_R=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{\lambda}J e_i.                  \tag{3}
130: \]
131: 
132: One must still prove that \(J\) has rank one; containment in
133: \(\mathbb C\) alone does not imply that. Let
134: \(r=\dim_{\mathbb Q}(\mathbb Q\otimes_R J)\), which is finite.
135: Tensoring (3) with the fraction field \(\mathbb Q\) and using the
136: rank \(n\) of \(M_R\) gives \(n=nr\), so \(r=1\), since \(n>0\).
137: The multiplication map \(\mathbb Q\otimes_R J\to\mathbb C\) is
138: injective: this tensor product is the localization of the torsion-free
139: module \(J\subset\mathbb C\), and a fraction mapping to zero has
140: zero numerator. Thus \(J\) spans a one-dimensional rational line.
141: 
142: Choose \(0\ne a\in J\) and write a finite set of nonzero generators
143: as \(q_1a,\ldots,q_ka\) with \(q_j\in\mathbb Q^\times\).
144: Each \(q_j=p^{\nu_j}u_j\) for \(\nu_j\in\mathbb Z\) and a unit
145: \(u_j\) of \(R\). Let \(\nu=\min_j\nu_j\). All generators belong
146: to \(p^\nu R a\), and a generator with minimal exponent generates
147: that whole module. Therefore \(J=Rb\) for a nonzero \(b\in J\).
148: By (3), \(b e_0,\ldots,b e_\lambda\) is an \(R\)-basis of \(M_R\).
149: 
150: ### 4. Reduce and extend scalars
151: 
152: All denominators in \(R\) are invertible in \(K\), so the integer map
153: extends to \(R\to K\). The natural tensor maps give
154: 
155: \[
156: M\otimes_{\mathbb Z}K\cong M_R\otimes_R K
157: \cong(M_R/pM_R)\otimes_{\mathbb F_p}K.
158: \]
159: 
160: For example the first map sends \(m\otimes c\) to
161: \((1\otimes m)\otimes c\); its inverse sends
162: \((r\otimes m)\otimes c\) to \(m\otimes\bar r c\).
163: The reduced images \(b_0,\ldots,b_\lambda\) of \(b e_i\) form a
164: \(K\)-basis, with exactly the matrices of step 1 reduced into \(K\).
165: The matrix-unit identities (2) persist on this basis.
166: 
167: For \(0\leq r\leq\lambda<p\), \(r!\ne0\) in \(K\), and the induced
168: \(X_r,Y_r\) equal \((r!)^{-1}x^r,(r!)^{-1}y^r\). Hence any
169: \(K\)-subspace invariant under \(x,y\) is invariant under every matrix
170: unit in (2).
171: 
172: ### 5. Conclude irreducibility
173: 
174: Let \(W\) be invariant. If it is nonzero, choose
175: \(0\ne w=\sum_i c_i b_i\in W\), and an index \(j\) with \(c_j\ne0\).
176: For every \(i\), \(E_{ij}w=c_jb_i\in W\). Division by \(c_j\)
177: gives \(b_i\in W\), so all basis vectors lie in \(W\) and
178: \(W=V(K)\). Since \(\dim_K V(K)=\lambda+1>0\), it is nonzero and
179: irreducible. If \(\lambda=0\), all relevant factorials and binomial
180: coefficients are one and the argument applies unchanged. For \(p=2\),
181: the allowed \(\lambda\) are zero and one; the proof still works
182: without requiring distinct reduced \(h\)-eigenvalues.
183: 
184: ## Input status
185: 
186: This file fixes the exercise, notation and supplied proof, including the
187: arbitrary-lattice argument. It is not an NL0 artifact, an Audit A receipt,
188: a Lean proof, or a passing test result. Future runs must construct and check
189: those artifacts from these explicit inputs, registering any foundational
190: module or localization results used by their NL0.

1: # Optional unconditional formalization
2: 
3: `--track full --formalization unconditional` selects
4: `2basis -> shared NL0/Audit A -> shared nl02lean/Audit B -> b2lean`.
5: The default is `conditional`; `full` still means both existing stages, not an
6: unconditional theorem. Existing jobs without `formalization` remain conditional.
7: Unconditional entry starts before NL0: accepted NL0 cannot skip the required
8: original-target/basis Audit A through `translate`.
9: 
10: ## Authority
11: 
12: The original selected target and documents remain immutable authority for H,
13: quantifiers, domains, parameters, normalizations, constant dependencies and any
14: specified algorithm. 2basis may change the proof route and representations.
15: The model chooses mathematical reductions. Python checks records, versions,
16: actual Lean proofs and interfaces; it does not certify source fidelity.
17: No difficulty scores, forced reduction tree or Mathlib-use whitelist apply.

Let \(p\) be any prime, \(K\) any field of characteristic \(p\), and
\(\lambda\) an integer with \(0\leq\lambda<p\).
Let \(V(\lambda)\) be the complex irreducible highest-weight
\(\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)\)-module of highest weight \(\lambda\),
of dimension \(\lambda+1\). Its Chevalley generators satisfy

\[
[h,x]=2x,\qquad[h,y]=-2y,\qquad[x,y]=h.
\]

Choose a nonzero highest-weight vector \(v\) with \(xv=0\) and
\(hv=\lambda v\). Let \(U_{\mathbb Z}\) be the integer subalgebra of
the universal enveloping algebra generated by all divided powers
\(X_r=x^r/r!\), \(Y_r=y^r/r!\), for integers \(r\geq0\).
An **admissible lattice** \(M\subset V(\lambda)\) is a free abelian
subgroup with an integer basis that is also a complex basis, stable under
\(U_{\mathbb Z}\). It is arbitrary, not necessarily the minimal lattice.

Put \(V(K)=M\otimes_{\mathbb Z}K\). The Lie algebra
\(L(K)=(\mathbb Zx+\mathbb Zy+\mathbb Zh)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}K\)
acts by the induced lattice operators. This is the Chevalley
\(\mathfrak{sl}_2\) construction also in characteristic 2.
Prove that \(V(K)\) is nonzero and every \(K\)-linear subspace
invariant under \(x,y,h\) is zero or all of \(V(K)\).
Both \(\lambda=0\) and \(p=2\) are included; \(K\) need not be
algebraically closed.

The selected full target and the original hypotheses H are unchanged. In particular p is any prime; K is any field of characteristic p, without an algebraic-closure assumption; lambda is an integer with 0≤lambda<p; V(lambda) is the given complex irreducible highest-weight sl2 module of dimension lambda+1; x,y,h and the nonzero highest-weight vector v have the stated normalization; and M is an arbitrary admissible lattice stable under every original divided power. Irreducibility of the complex module is retained as an original hypothesis, though the following argument only needs its stated dimension and highest-weight data. No new assumption on M is introduced.

We use ell=lambda.toNat, so the original inequality 0≤lambda gives lambda=(ell:Z), and the range becomes ell<p. All coefficients ell−2i in complex or integer formulas mean integer subtraction, even when negative. Index sets {0,...,ell} mean Fin(ell+1); factorials and binomial coefficients are those of natural numbers. Endomorphism products act on the rightmost argument first. Write X_r=(r!)^(-1)x^r and Y_r=(r!)^(-1)y^r exactly as in the problem; the definitions dividedPower and Stable are recorded in lean_header. The header's AdmissibleLattice packages a choice of the original common integer/complex basis indexed by Fin n. This packaging is justified below by B007, rather than assumed for a special lattice.

The native foundational propositions are B001 (independent families of the correct finite size span), B002 (a free integer basis extends to a field basis), B003 (factorials of indices below p have nonzero image), B004 (the binomial/factorial identity), B006 (basis expansion and determination of endomorphisms), and B007 (finiteness and cardinality of any basis in finite dimension). B005 is the prepared closed compatibility adapter for scalar extension of endomorphisms as a ring homomorphism. Their actual closed Lean proofs accompany the registry. We now give the recursive internal derivations; these class-3 facts are to be proved internally in the later NL0/Lean work, not supplied as external premises.

B101: characteristic-zero coordinates, including termination.

For every i≥0, the relations hy=yh−2y and xy=yx+h give
  h y^i v=(ell−2i)y^i v,
  x y^(i+1)v=(i+1)(ell−i)y^i v.
The first identity follows by induction from hv=ell v. For the second, the base i=0 is xyv=yxv+hv=ell v. If xy^i v=i(ell−i+1)y^(i−1)v, then
  xy^(i+1)v=y(xy^i v)+hy^i v
            =[i(ell−i+1)+(ell−2i)]y^i v
            =(i+1)(ell−i)y^i v.
Thus this induction does not use any termination assertion.

For 0≤i≤ell, applying x repeatedly gives
  x^i y^i v=[product_(r=1,...,i) r(ell−r+1)]v.
Every factor is a positive integer if i>0 and hence is nonzero in C; for i=0 the product is 1. Since v≠0, y^i v≠0. Define e_i=y^i v/i!, which is also nonzero. The eigenvalues a_i=ell−2i are pairwise distinct in C: equality would imply 2(i−j)=0 in characteristic zero and hence i=j.

To prove independence, take a relation sum_i z_i e_i=0 and fix j. Apply the composition product_(k≠j)(h−a_k Id). Each e_i with i≠j is killed by the factor k=i. The surviving term is
  z_j [product_(k≠j)(a_j−a_k)] e_j=0.
Every scalar factor and e_j is nonzero, so z_j=0. This works for every j and includes the singleton index set. By B001 the ell+1 vectors span V of dimension ell+1, and independence together with spanning defines a basis.

The first recurrence also makes z=y^(ell+1)v an h-eigenvector with eigenvalue a=−ell−2 (the vector z is permitted to be zero). Expand z in this basis using B006. Applying h−a Id gives
  sum_i z_i(a_i−a)e_i=0.
For i≤ell, a_i−a=2(ell+1−i)≠0 in C. Independence gives every z_i=0, so z=0. All higher lowering powers vanish as well. Dividing the recurrences by i!, and using (i+1)!=(i+1)i!, now gives exactly
  xe_0=0; xe_i=(ell−i+1)e_(i−1) for 1≤i≤ell;
  ye_i=(i+1)e_(i+1) for i<ell; ye_ell=0;
  he_i=(ell−2i)e_i.
For r≤i, iterating x gives the coefficient product_(s=1,...,r)(ell−i+s) on e_(i−r). Division by r! gives choose(ell−i+r,r), by B004 with n=ell−i+r and j=r and cancellation of the nonzero factorial (ell−i)!. If r>i, the lowering in index reaches e_0 and is then killed by x. For i+r≤ell, iterating y gives (i+r)!/i! on e_(i+r); division by r! gives choose(i+r,r) by B004. If i+r>ell, the string reaches e_ell and is killed by y. These are precisely the divided-power formulas for all r, including r=0. This proves B101 from B001, B004, and B006.

B102: integral scaled matrix units on the arbitrary lattice.

Admissibility says that every X_r and Y_r carries M into M. Their restrictions X_r^M,Y_r^M are Z-linear endomorphisms. The inclusion M→V is injective, since M is an actual subgroup; it intertwines each restricted operator with the corresponding complex operator. In particular x_M=X_1^M and y_M=Y_1^M are the original x,y restricted to M. Since h=xy−yx, h also restricts and equals x_M y_M−y_M x_M. For each r≥0 the defining complex identity r! X_r=x^r, and injectivity of M→V, give the integer endomorphism identity r! X_r^M=x_M^r, and likewise for Y_r^M and y_M. Here integer multiples are repeated addition of endomorphisms, not division in M.

Use the B101 basis to define E_ij in End_C(V) by E_ij e_k=e_i if k=j and zero otherwise. Define
  P=Y_ell X_ell,    c_j=choose(ell,j),
  A_ij^C=X_(ell−i) P Y_(ell−j).
The divided-power formulas give P=E_(ell,ell): X_ell kills each e_k with k<ell, while it sends e_ell to e_0, and Y_ell sends e_0 to e_ell. They also give X_(ell−i) P=E_(i,ell), since X_(ell−i)e_ell=e_i.

For P Y_(ell−j), examine an input e_k. If k<j, its image under Y_(ell−j) has index below ell and is killed by P. If k>j it is sent beyond the end and is zero already. If k=j its image is choose(ell,ell−j)e_ell=c_j e_ell. The equality of the two binomial coefficients follows from B004 for j and ell−j by cancellation of the equal nonzero factorial products in the integers. Consequently
  P Y_(ell−j)=c_j E_(ell,j),   A_ij^C=c_j E_ij.
Each equality is established on all basis vectors and hence is an endomorphism equality by B006.

The same product of restricted divided powers defines
  P_M=Y_ell^M X_ell^M,   A_ij=X_(ell−i)^M P_M Y_(ell−j)^M
in End_Z(M). Thus the restriction of A_ij^C is A_ij; no assertion that E_ij itself preserves M over Z is being made.

The coordinate matrix units obey E_ij E_kl=E_il if j=k and zero otherwise. Multiplying the scaled formulas therefore gives
  A_ij^C A_kl^C=c_j A_il^C if j=k, and zero otherwise.
Indeed, when j=k, the left side is c_j c_l E_il and A_il^C=c_l E_il. Put
  D=product_(j=0,...,ell)c_j,
  d_j=product_(k=0,...,ell; k≠j)c_k.
Then d_j c_j=D, including the singleton case. On each e_k one has
  (sum_j d_j A_jj^C)e_k=D e_k,
so B006 gives sum_j d_j A_jj^C=D Id_V. All coefficients are integers and all operators in these identities preserve M. Composing with the injective inclusion of M into V proves in End_Z(M) that
  A_ij A_kl= c_j A_il if j=k, and zero otherwise,
  sum_j d_j A_jj=D Id_M.
This proves B102. It uses no localization, rationality of lattice coordinates, fractional ideals, or classification of modules over a discrete valuation ring.

B104: match the original tensor product and compute its dimension.

The given Z-basis of M, after inclusion into V, is a complex basis. Apply B007 to that complex basis: its index type is finite and has cardinality dim_C V=ell+1. Choose a bijection with Fin(ell+1) and reindex both the Z-basis and the complex basis by the same bijection. Their inclusion relation is unchanged. This is exactly the header's AdmissibleLattice with n=ell+1, and works for every original admissible lattice.

Let U=K⊗_Z M. By B002, U has a K-basis q_i=1⊗m_i indexed by Fin(ell+1), and dim_K U=ell+1. It is nonzero: q_0 cannot be zero, since its basis coordinate at 0 is 1 and 1≠0 in K. This supplies nonzeroness without assuming that M has a special basis related to the e_i.

For completeness define S:M⊗_Z K→K⊗_Z M by
  S(m⊗a)=a⊗m,
and S_inv in the other direction by S_inv(a⊗m)=m⊗a. Both displayed rules are additive in each variable and balanced over Z, because moving an integer scalar between the tensor factors has the same effect on either side. The defining universal property of the tensor product therefore gives additive maps. Give M⊗_Z K its usual K-action on the second factor and U its K-action on the first factor. For b∈K,
  S(b·(m⊗a))=S(m⊗ba)=ba⊗m=b·S(m⊗a);
the same calculation proves K-linearity of S_inv. Their composites fix every pure tensor, and every tensor is a finite sum of pure tensors, so they are mutual inverses. This is a concrete K-linear isomorphism, rather than an additional tensor-associativity premise.

For f∈End_Z(M), its original induced operator f_K on M⊗K is defined on pure tensors by f_K(m⊗a)=f(m)⊗a. The same balanced-bilinear verification makes this well-defined and K-linear. B005 gives F(f)(a⊗m)=a⊗f(m), hence
  S(f_K(m⊗a))=a⊗f(m)=F(f)(S(m⊗a)).
Again equality on pure tensors gives S f_K=F(f) S everywhere. In particular this applies to x_M,y_M,h_M and every divided power. Thus invariant subspaces and the zero and whole spaces correspond under S, and the original tensor product is nonzero. This proves B104 from B002, B005, and B007.

B103: reduction and normalized matrix units; invariant subspaces remain stable.

Apply B005 to M and K and write F for its unital ring homomorphism. A bar on a natural or integer coefficient means its image in K. B003 gives overline(ell!)≠0, because ell<p. For 0≤j≤ell, B004 gives in K
  cbar_j · overline(j!) · overline((ell−j)!)=overline(ell!)≠0.
A product equal to a nonzero element of a field has no zero factor, so cbar_j≠0. Thus Dbar=product_j cbar_j≠0. Define
  T_ij=(cbar_j)^(-1) F(A_ij) ∈ End_K(U).
The ring homomorphism F preserves finite sums, products, the identity, and integer multiples. For clarity integer multiples can be expressed by repeated addition and negation of the identity and multiplication; preservation follows from the RingHom laws. In End_K(U), integer multiplication of an endomorphism is the same as scalar multiplication by its image in K.

Apply F to the multiplication identities of B102. If j≠k then T_ij T_kl=0. If j=k then
  T_ij T_kl
   =(cbar_j)^(-1)(cbar_l)^(-1) F(c_j A_il)
   =(cbar_l)^(-1) F(A_il)=T_il.
All scalar inverses used here exist by the preceding nonvanishing. Apply F to the sum identity:
  sum_j dbar_j F(A_jj)=Dbar Id_U.
Since dbar_j cbar_j=Dbar and both cbar_j and Dbar are nonzero, division by Dbar gives
  sum_j T_jj=Id_U.
Thus these are actual matrix-unit relations on U; their construction and proof do not need a coordinate identification of the reduced arbitrary lattice with the characteristic-zero e_i.

Now let W be a K-subspace of U invariant under x'=F(x_M) and y'=F(y_M). Induction on r shows that it is invariant under (x')^r and (y')^r, including the identity at r=0. For every 0≤r≤ell, B003 gives overline(r!)≠0. Applying F to the B102 factorial identities, and using preservation of powers, yields
  F(X_r^M)=overline(r!)^(-1)(x')^r,
  F(Y_r^M)=overline(r!)^(-1)(y')^r.
Because W is K-linear, it is invariant under these scalar multiples. Each A_ij uses only indices ell−i,ell,ell−j between 0 and ell, so its image under F is a composition of operators preserving W. Finally scalar multiplication by cbar_j^(-1) also preserves W, proving that all T_ij preserve W. This proves B103 from B003, B004, B005, and B102. It does not infer stability of divided powers from Lie invariance for any index at or above p.

B105: the finite matrix-unit irreducibility argument.

Let K be any field, n>0, dim_K U=n, and let endomorphisms T_ij, indexed by Fin n, have the displayed multiplication and diagonal-sum relations. Suppose W is stable under them and W≠0. Choose w∈W with w≠0. Since w=sum_j T_jj w, there exists j with u=T_jj w≠0. Stability gives u∈W, and the relation T_jj^2=T_jj gives T_jj u=u.

For each i set u_i=T_ij u. These n vectors belong to W. If sum_i a_i u_i=0, fix k and apply T_jk. The multiplication relation gives
  0=sum_i a_i T_jk T_ij u=a_k T_jj u=a_k u.
Since u≠0 and K is a field, a_k=0. Every k has zero coefficient, so the family (u_i) is linearly independent. Its index cardinality n equals dim_K U; B001 therefore gives span_K{u_i}=U. As W contains every u_i, it contains their span and equals U. Together with the alternative W=0, this proves B105. This argument is valid even when the image of n in K is zero; it never divides by n or takes traces.

B106: the complete original target.

Take the original arbitrary admissible lattice, prime p, field K, and integer lambda, and use ell as at the start. B104 gives a nonzero U=K⊗_Z M of dimension ell+1 and an intertwining K-linear isomorphism S from the originally specified V(K)=M⊗_Z K. The induced x,y,h operators are precisely those in the problem: h restricts by [x,y]=h, and scalar extension of their integral restrictions preserves all three given Chevalley commutator relations. In particular this is still the stipulated Chevalley action in characteristic 2; no alternative definition using a quotient by a scalar element or a characteristic-dependent identification is used. The construction of the Lie algebra tensor and its action is just Z-bilinear extension of these operators, so invariance under its generators is the stipulated x,y,h invariance.

Let W be any K-linear subspace of V(K) invariant under x,y,h. Its image S(W) is K-linear and invariant under x'=F(x_M) and y'=F(y_M), by the intertwining identities. B103 supplies endomorphisms T_ij satisfying the matrix-unit relations and preserving S(W). Apply B105 with n=ell+1>0. It gives S(W)=0 or S(W)=U; applying the inverse isomorphism gives W=0 or W=V(K). B104 already proves V(K)≠0. This proves every clause of the full target.

If lambda=0, the sole index is 0, X_0=Y_0=Id, c_0=D=d_0=1, and the same construction and proof apply. If p=2, ell is 0 or 1, and all factorials actually inverted have index below 2; the argument never asks for distinct h-eigenvalues in K. All eigenvalue separation occurred only in the original characteristic-zero space. No algebraic closure of K, choice of a minimal lattice, or additional hypothesis on p is used.

Its injection and rank facts for Z_(p)⊗M, coordinate modules J_i, equality of all J_i, dimension computation for Q⊗J, injectivity of its multiplication map, and principal fractional-ideal/valuation argument are unnecessary because B102 gives integer polynomial endomorphism identities and B103 reduces them directly. The original invariant-subspace argument requiring a common scaled e_i lattice basis is replaced by B105's dimension argument for abstract matrix units. namespace YuiBasisObjects

noncomputable def dividedPower {V : Type*} [AddCommGroup V] [Module ℂ V]
    (f : Module.End ℂ V) (r : ℕ) : Module.End ℂ V :=
  ((r.factorial : ℂ)⁻¹) • f ^ r

def Stable {K V : Type*} [Field K] [AddCommGroup V] [Module K V]
    (W : Submodule K V) (f : Module.End K V) : Prop :=
  ∀ w, w ∈ W → f w ∈ W

structure AdmissibleLattice (n : ℕ) (V : Type*) [AddCommGroup V] [Module ℂ V]
    (x y : Module.End ℂ V) where
  carrier : Submodule ℤ V
  zBasis : Module.Basis (Fin n) ℤ carrier
  cBasis : Module.Basis (Fin n) ℂ V
  coe_basis : ∀ i, (zBasis i : V) = cBasis i
  stableX : ∀ (r : ℕ) (m : V), m ∈ carrier → dividedPower x r m ∈ carrier
  stableY : ∀ (r : ℕ) (m : V), m ∈ carrier → dividedPower y r m ∈ carrier

13: /-!
14: # Invertibility of factorials
15: 
16: This file contains lemmas providing sufficient conditions for the cast of `n!` to a (semi)ring `A`
17: to be a unit.
18: 
19: -/

23: namespace IsUnit

25: open Nat
26: section Semiring

28: variable {A : Type*} [Semiring A]
29: 
30: theorem natCast_factorial_of_le {n : ℕ} (hn_fac : IsUnit (n ! : A))
31:     {m : ℕ} (hmn : m ≤ n) : IsUnit (m ! : A) := by
32:   obtain ⟨k, rfl⟩ := exists_add_of_le hmn
33:   clear hmn
34:   induction k generalizing m with
35:   | zero => simpa using hn_fac
36:   | succ k ih =>
37:     rw [← add_assoc, add_right_comm] at hn_fac
38:     have := ih hn_fac
39:     rw [Nat.factorial_succ, Nat.cast_mul, Nat.cast_commute _ _ |>.isUnit_mul_iff] at this
40:     exact this.2
41: 
42: theorem natCast_factorial_of_lt {n : ℕ} (hn_fac : IsUnit ((n - 1)! : A))
43:     {m : ℕ} (hmn : m < n) : IsUnit (m ! : A) :=
44:   hn_fac.natCast_factorial_of_le <| le_sub_one_of_lt hmn
45: 
46: /-- If `A` is an algebra over a characteristic-zero (semi)field, then `n!` is a unit. -/
47: theorem natCast_factorial_of_algebra (K : Type*) [Semifield K] [CharZero K] [Algebra K A] (n : ℕ) :
48:     IsUnit (n ! : A) := by
49:   suffices IsUnit (n ! : K) by
50:     simpa using this.map (algebraMap K A)
51:   simp [isUnit_iff_ne_zero, n.factorial_ne_zero]
52: 
53: end Semiring

57: variable {A : Type*} [Ring A] (p : ℕ) [Fact (Nat.Prime p)] [CharP A p]

59: theorem natCast_factorial_iff_of_charP {n : ℕ} : IsUnit (n ! : A) ↔ n < p := by
60:   have hp : p.Prime := Fact.out
61:   induction n with
62:   | zero => simp [hp.pos]
63:   | succ n ih =>
64:     -- TODO: why is `.symm.symm` needed here!?
65:     rw [factorial_succ, cast_mul, Nat.cast_commute _ _ |>.isUnit_mul_iff, ih.symm.symm,
66:       ← Nat.add_one_le_iff, CharP.isUnit_natCast_iff hp]
67:     exact ⟨fun ⟨h1, h2⟩ ↦ lt_of_le_of_ne h2 (mt (· ▸ dvd_rfl) h1),
68:       fun h ↦ ⟨not_dvd_of_pos_of_lt (Nat.succ_pos _) h, h.le⟩⟩
69: 
70: end CharP

77: lemma natCast_of_isNilpotent_of_coprime (h : p.Coprime n) :
78:     IsUnit (n : A) := by
79:   obtain ⟨m, hm⟩ := hp
80:   suffices ∃ a b : A, p ^ m * a + n * b = 1 by
81:     obtain ⟨a, b, h⟩ := this
82:     refine .of_mul_eq_one b ?_
83:     simpa [hm] using h
84:   refine ⟨(p ^ m).gcdA n, (p ^ m).gcdB n, ?_⟩
85:   norm_cast
86:   rw [← Nat.cast_one, ← Int.cast_natCast 1, ← (h.pow_left m).gcd_eq_one, Nat.gcd_eq_gcd_ab]
87: 
88: theorem natCast_factorial_of_isNilpotent [Fact p.Prime] (h : n < p) :
89:     IsUnit (n ! : A) := by
90:   induction n with
91:   | zero => simp
92:   | succ n ih =>
93:     simp only [factorial_succ, cast_mul, IsUnit.mul_iff]
94:     refine ⟨.natCast_of_isNilpotent_of_coprime hp ?_, ih (by lia)⟩
95:     rw [Nat.Prime.coprime_iff_not_dvd Fact.out]
96:     exact Nat.not_dvd_of_pos_of_lt (by lia) h
97: 
98: end Nilpotent

125: theorem choose_ne_zero_iff {n k : ℕ} : n.choose k ≠ 0 ↔ k ≤ n :=
126:   not_iff_not.1 <| by simp [choose_eq_zero_iff]

128: lemma choose_ne_zero {n k : ℕ} (h : k ≤ n) : n.choose k ≠ 0 :=
129:   (choose_pos h).ne'
130: 
131: theorem add_one_mul_choose_eq : ∀ n k, (n + 1) * choose n k = choose (n + 1) (k + 1) * (k + 1)
132:   | 0, 0 => by decide
133:   | 0, k + 1 => by simp [choose]
134:   | n + 1, 0 => by simp [choose, mul_succ, Nat.add_comm]
135:   | n + 1, k + 1 => by
136:     rw [choose_succ_succ' (n + 1) (k + 1), Nat.add_mul _ _ (k + 1 + 1), ← add_one_mul_choose_eq n,
137:       mul_add_one, ← add_one_mul_choose_eq n, Nat.add_right_comm _ _ (_ * _), ← Nat.mul_add,
138:       ← choose_succ_succ', ← add_one_mul]
139: 
140: @[deprecated add_one_mul_choose_eq (since := "2025-12-09")]
141: theorem succ_mul_choose_eq : ∀ n k, succ n * choose n k = choose (succ n) (succ k) * succ k :=
142:   add_one_mul_choose_eq
143: 
144: theorem choose_mul_factorial_mul_factorial : ∀ {n k}, k ≤ n → choose n k * k ! * (n - k)! = n !
145:   | 0, _, hk => by simp [Nat.eq_zero_of_le_zero hk]
146:   | n + 1, 0, _ => by simp
147:   | n + 1, succ k, hk => by
148:     rcases lt_or_eq_of_le hk with hk₁ | hk₁
149:     · have h : choose n k * k.succ ! * (n - k)! = (k + 1) * n ! := by
150:         rw [← choose_mul_factorial_mul_factorial (le_of_succ_le_succ hk)]
151:         simp [factorial_succ, Nat.mul_comm, Nat.mul_left_comm, Nat.mul_assoc]
152:       have h₁ : (n - k)! = (n - k) * (n - k.succ)! := by
153:         rw [← succ_sub_succ, succ_sub (le_of_lt_succ hk₁), factorial_succ]
154:       have h₂ : choose n (succ k) * k.succ ! * ((n - k) * (n - k.succ)!) = (n - k) * n ! := by
155:         rw [← choose_mul_factorial_mul_factorial (le_of_lt_succ hk₁)]
156:         simp [factorial_succ, Nat.mul_comm, Nat.mul_left_comm, Nat.mul_assoc]
157:       have h₃ : k * n ! ≤ n * n ! := Nat.mul_le_mul_right _ (le_of_succ_le_succ hk)
158:       rw [choose_succ_succ, Nat.add_mul, Nat.add_mul, succ_sub_succ, h, h₁, h₂, Nat.add_mul,
159:         Nat.mul_sub_right_distrib, factorial_succ, ← Nat.add_sub_assoc h₃, Nat.add_assoc,
160:         ← Nat.add_mul, Nat.add_sub_cancel_left, Nat.add_comm]
161:     · rw [hk₁]; simp [Nat.mul_comm, choose, Nat.sub_self]
162: 
163: theorem choose_mul {n k s : ℕ} (hsk : s ≤ k) :
164:     n.choose k * k.choose s = n.choose s * (n - s).choose (k - s) := by
165:   obtain hnk | hkn := lt_or_ge n k
166:   · grind

11: /-!
12: # Bases
13: 
14: This file defines bases in a module or vector space.
15: 
16: It is inspired by Isabelle/HOL's linear algebra, and hence indirectly by HOL Light.
17: 
18: ## Main definitions
19: 
20: All definitions are given for families of vectors, i.e. `v : ι → M` where `M` is the module or
21: vector space and `ι : Type*` is an arbitrary indexing type.
22: 
23: * `Basis ι R M` is the type of `ι`-indexed `R`-bases for a module `M`,
24:   represented by a linear equiv `M ≃ₗ[R] ι →₀ R`.
25: * the basis vectors of a basis `b : Basis ι R M` are available as `b i`, where `i : ι`
26: 
27: * `Basis.repr` is the isomorphism sending `x : M` to its coordinates `Basis.repr x : ι →₀ R`.
28:   The converse, turning this isomorphism into a basis, is called `Basis.ofRepr`.
29: * If `ι` is finite, there is a variant of `repr` called `Basis.equivFun b : M ≃ₗ[R] ι → R`
30:   (saving you from having to work with `Finsupp`). The converse, turning this isomorphism into
31:   a basis, is called `Basis.ofEquivFun`.
32: 
33: * `Basis.reindex` uses an equiv to map a basis to a different indexing set.
34: 
35: * `Basis.map` uses a linear equiv to map a basis to a different module.
36: 
37: * `Basis.constr`: given `b : Basis ι R M` and `f : ι → M`, construct a linear map `g` so that
38:   `g (b i) = f i`.
39: 
40: * `Basis.coord`: `b.coord i x` is the `i`-th coordinate of a vector `x` with respect to the basis
41:   `b`.
42: 
43: ## Main results
44: 
45: * `Basis.ext` states that two linear maps are equal if they coincide on a basis.
46:   Similar results are available for linear equivs (if they coincide on the basis vectors),
47:   elements (if their coordinates coincide) and the functions `b.repr` and `⇑b`.
48: 
49: ## Implementation notes
50: 
51: We use families instead of sets because it allows us to say that two identical vectors are linearly
52: dependent. For bases, this is useful as well because we can easily derive ordered bases by using an
53: ordered index type `ι`.
54: 
55: ## Tags
56: 
57: basis, bases
58: 
59: -/

82: /-- A `Basis ι R M` for a module `M` is the type of `ι`-indexed `R`-bases of `M`.
83: 
84: The basis vectors are available as `DFunLike.coe (b : Basis ι R M) : ι → M`.
85: To turn a linear independent family of vectors spanning `M` into a basis, use `Basis.mk`.
86: They are internally represented as linear equivs `M ≃ₗ[R] (ι →₀ R)`,
87: available as `Basis.repr`.

90: structure Basis where
91:   /-- `Basis.ofRepr` constructs a basis given an assignment of coordinates to each vector. -/
92:   ofRepr ::
93:     /-- `repr` is the linear equivalence sending a vector `x` to its coordinates:
94:     the `c`s such that `x = ∑ i, c i`. -/
95:     repr : M ≃ₗ[R] ι →₀ R

99: instance : Inhabited (Basis ι R (ι →₀ R)) :=
100:   ⟨.ofRepr (LinearEquiv.refl _ _)⟩

106: theorem repr_injective : Injective (repr : Basis ι R M → M ≃ₗ[R] ι →₀ R) := fun f g h => by
107:   cases f; cases g; congr
108: 
109: /-- `b i` is the `i`th basis vector. -/
110: instance instFunLike : FunLike (Basis ι R M) ι M where
111:   coe b i := b.repr.symm (Finsupp.single i 1)
112:   coe_injective f g h := repr_injective <| LinearEquiv.symm_bijective.injective <|
113:     LinearEquiv.toLinearMap_injective <| by ext; exact congr_fun h _

115: @[simp]
116: theorem coe_ofRepr (e : M ≃ₗ[R] ι →₀ R) : ⇑(ofRepr e) = fun i => e.symm (Finsupp.single i 1) :=
117:   rfl
118: 
119: protected theorem injective [Nontrivial R] : Injective b :=
120:   b.repr.symm.injective.comp fun _ _ => (Finsupp.single_left_inj (one_ne_zero : (1 : R) ≠ 0)).mp
121: 
122: theorem repr_symm_single_one : b.repr.symm (Finsupp.single i 1) = b i :=
123:   rfl
124: 
125: theorem repr_symm_single : b.repr.symm (Finsupp.single i c) = c • b i :=
126:   calc
127:     b.repr.symm (Finsupp.single i c) = b.repr.symm (c • Finsupp.single i (1 : R)) := by
128:       { rw [Finsupp.smul_single', mul_one] }
129:     _ = c • b i := by rw [map_smul, repr_symm_single_one]
130: 
131: @[simp]
132: theorem repr_self : b.repr (b i) = Finsupp.single i 1 :=
133:   LinearEquiv.apply_symm_apply _ _
134: 
135: theorem repr_self_apply (j) [Decidable (i = j)] : b.repr (b i) j = if i = j then 1 else 0 := by
136:   rw [repr_self, Finsupp.single_apply]
137: 
138: @[simp]
139: theorem repr_symm_apply (v) : b.repr.symm v = Finsupp.linearCombination R b v :=
140:   calc
141:     b.repr.symm v = b.repr.symm (v.sum Finsupp.single) := by simp
142:     _ = v.sum fun i vi => b.repr.symm (Finsupp.single i vi) := map_finsuppSum ..
143:     _ = Finsupp.linearCombination R b v := by simp only [repr_symm_single,
144:                                                          Finsupp.linearCombination_apply]

146: @[simp]
147: theorem coe_repr_symm : ↑b.repr.symm = Finsupp.linearCombination R b :=
148:   LinearMap.ext fun v => b.repr_symm_apply v
149: 
150: @[simp]
151: theorem repr_linearCombination (v) : b.repr (Finsupp.linearCombination _ b v) = v := by
152:   rw [← b.coe_repr_symm]
153:   exact b.repr.apply_symm_apply v
154: 
155: @[simp]
156: theorem linearCombination_repr : Finsupp.linearCombination _ b (b.repr x) = x := by
157:   rw [← b.coe_repr_symm]
158:   exact b.repr.symm_apply_apply x

185: /-- `b.reindex (e : ι ≃ ι')` is a basis indexed by `ι'` -/
186: def reindex : Basis ι' R M :=
187:   .ofRepr (b.repr.trans (Finsupp.domLCongr e))
188: 
189: theorem reindex_apply (i' : ι') : b.reindex e i' = b (e.symm i') :=
190:   show (b.repr.trans (Finsupp.domLCongr e)).symm (Finsupp.single i' 1) =
191:     b.repr.symm (Finsupp.single (e.symm i') 1)
192:   by rw [LinearEquiv.symm_trans_apply, Finsupp.domLCongr_symm, Finsupp.domLCongr_single]

194: @[simp]
195: theorem coe_reindex : (b.reindex e : ι' → M) = b ∘ e.symm :=
196:   funext (b.reindex_apply e)
197: 
198: theorem repr_reindex_apply (i' : ι') : (b.reindex e).repr x i' = b.repr x (e.symm i') :=
199:   show (Finsupp.domLCongr e : _ ≃ₗ[R] _) (b.repr x) i' = _ by simp
200: 
201: @[simp]
202: theorem repr_reindex : (b.reindex e).repr x = (b.repr x).mapDomain e :=
203:   DFunLike.ext _ _ <| by simp [repr_reindex_apply]
204: 
205: @[simp]
206: theorem reindex_refl : b.reindex (Equiv.refl ι) = b := by
207:   simp [reindex]

209: /-- `simp` can prove this as `Basis.coe_reindex` + `EquivLike.range_comp` -/
210: theorem range_reindex : Set.range (b.reindex e) = Set.range b := by
211:   simp [coe_reindex, range_comp]

223: /-- A module over `R` with a finite basis is linearly equivalent to functions from its basis to `R`.
224: -/
225: def Basis.equivFun [Finite ι] (b : Basis ι R M) : M ≃ₗ[R] ι → R :=
226:   LinearEquiv.trans b.repr
227:     ({ Finsupp.equivFunOnFinite with
228:         toFun := (↑)
229:         map_add' := Finsupp.coe_add
230:         map_smul' := Finsupp.coe_smul } :
231:       (ι →₀ R) ≃ₗ[R] ι → R)
232: 
233: /-- A module over a finite ring that admits a finite basis is finite. -/
234: @[implicit_reducible]
235: def fintypeOfFintype [Fintype ι] (b : Basis ι R M) [Fintype R] : Fintype M :=
236:   haveI := Classical.decEq ι
237:   Fintype.ofEquiv _ b.equivFun.toEquiv.symm
238: 
239: /-- Given a basis `v` indexed by `ι`, the canonical linear equivalence between `ι → R` and `M` maps
240: a function `x : ι → R` to the linear combination `∑_i x i • v i`. -/
241: @[simp]
242: theorem Basis.equivFun_symm_apply [Fintype ι] (b : Basis ι R M) (x : ι → R) :
243:     b.equivFun.symm x = ∑ i, x i • b i := by
244:   simp [Basis.equivFun, Finsupp.linearCombination_apply, sum_fintype, equivFunOnFinite]
245: 
246: @[simp]
247: theorem Basis.equivFun_apply [Finite ι] (b : Basis ι R M) (u : M) : b.equivFun u = b.repr u :=
248:   rfl
249: 
250: @[simp]
251: theorem Basis.map_equivFun [Finite ι] (b : Basis ι R M) (f : M ≃ₗ[R] M') :
252:     (b.map f).equivFun = f.symm.trans b.equivFun :=
253:   rfl
254: 
255: theorem Basis.sum_equivFun [Fintype ι] (b : Basis ι R M) (u : M) :
256:     ∑ i, b.equivFun u i • b i = u := by
257:   rw [← b.equivFun_symm_apply, b.equivFun.symm_apply_apply]
258: 
259: @[simp]
260: theorem Basis.sum_repr [Fintype ι] (b : Basis ι R M) (u : M) : ∑ i, b.repr u i • b i = u :=
261:   b.sum_equivFun u
262: 
263: @[simp]
264: theorem Basis.equivFun_self [Finite ι] [DecidableEq ι] (b : Basis ι R M) (i j : ι) :
265:     b.equivFun (b i) j = if i = j then 1 else 0 := by rw [b.equivFun_apply, b.repr_self_apply]
266: 
267: theorem Basis.repr_sum_self [Fintype ι] (b : Basis ι R M) (c : ι → R) :
268:     b.repr (∑ i, c i • b i) = c := by
269:   simp_rw [← b.equivFun_symm_apply, ← b.equivFun_apply, b.equivFun.apply_symm_apply]
270: 
271: /-- Define a basis by mapping each vector `x : M` to its coordinates `e x : ι → R`,
272: as long as `ι` is finite. -/
273: def Basis.ofEquivFun [Finite ι] (e : M ≃ₗ[R] ι → R) : Basis ι R M :=
274:   .ofRepr <| e.trans <| LinearEquiv.symm <| Finsupp.linearEquivFunOnFinite R R ι
275: 
276: @[simp]
277: theorem Basis.ofEquivFun_repr_apply [Finite ι] (e : M ≃ₗ[R] ι → R) (x : M) (i : ι) :
278:     (Basis.ofEquivFun e).repr x i = e x i :=
279:   rfl
280: 
281: @[simp]
282: theorem Basis.coe_ofEquivFun [Finite ι] [DecidableEq ι] (e : M ≃ₗ[R] ι → R) :
283:     (Basis.ofEquivFun e : ι → M) = fun i => e.symm (Pi.single i 1) :=
284:   funext fun i =>
285:     e.injective <|
286:       funext fun j => by
287:         simp [Basis.ofEquivFun, ← Finsupp.single_eq_pi_single]
288: 
289: @[simp]
290: theorem Basis.ofEquivFun_equivFun [Finite ι] (v : Basis ι R M) :
291:     Basis.ofEquivFun v.equivFun = v :=
292:   Basis.repr_injective <| by ext; rfl
293: 
294: @[simp]
295: theorem Basis.equivFun_ofEquivFun [Finite ι] (e : M ≃ₗ[R] ι → R) :
296:     (Basis.ofEquivFun e).equivFun = e := by
297:   ext j
298:   simp_rw [Basis.equivFun_apply, Basis.ofEquivFun_repr_apply]
299: 
300: end Fintype

15: # Lemmas about rank and `finrank` in rings satisfying strong rank condition.
16: 
17: ## Main statements
18: 
19: For modules over rings satisfying the rank condition
20: 
21: * `Basis.le_span`:
22:   the cardinality of a basis is bounded by the cardinality of any spanning set
23: 
24: For modules over rings satisfying the strong rank condition
25: 
26: * `linearIndependent_le_span`:
27:   For any linearly independent family `v : ι → M`
28:   and any finite spanning set `w : Set M`,
29:   the cardinality of `ι` is bounded by the cardinality of `w`.
30: * `linearIndependent_le_basis`:
31:   If `b` is a basis for a module `M`,
32:   and `s` is a linearly independent set,
33:   then the cardinality of `s` is bounded by the cardinality of `b`.
34: 
35: For modules over rings with invariant basis number
36: (including all commutative rings and all Noetherian rings)
37: 
38: * `mk_eq_mk_of_basis`: the dimension theorem, any two bases of the same vector space have the same
39:   cardinality.
40: 
41: ## Additional definition
42: 
43: * `Algebra.IsQuadraticExtension`: An extension of rings `R ⊆ S` is quadratic if `S` is a
44:   free `R`-algebra of rank `2`.
